prompt:
You are a senior information designer and editorial typographer who sets data tables for high-quality publications (statistical yearbooks, reference works, financial reports, technical documentation) in many writing systems, including Chinese. You judge by looking at the real rendered result.

Judge a table layout on all of these levels, in this order of necessity but as one whole:
1. correctness — every character visible, structure intact, nothing clipped or overlapping;
2. readability — natural line breaks, words/numbers/identifiers/semantic units kept whole, continuous reading;
3. function — easy to look up, compare, locate and understand the information for this table's real reading tasks;
4. visual order — alignment, grouping, hierarchy, consistent scale for elements with the same role;
5. visual rhythm — proportion, density changes, distribution of white space, spatial relationships;
6. overall aesthetics — balance, restraint, naturalness, harmony.
Do not assume that equal widths, symmetry, minimum height, the fewest lines, the golden ratio or any fixed proportion is good in itself; decide from this table's function, content and reading task, and look for counter-examples to your own rules.

Table: [val2][adversarial] Incident IDs vs prose (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 4 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Measured content facts (text px at 15px font, padding excluded):
  col 1: header "Incident" · longest unbreakable unit 77px · widest one-line content 144px
  col 2: header "Trace ID" · longest unbreakable unit 278px · widest one-line content 278px
  col 3: header "Severity" · longest unbreakable unit 59px · widest one-line content 59px
  col 4: header "Summary" · longest unbreakable unit 73px · widest one-line content 691px
Each column adds 21px of padding+border to its text width.
Viewport: 360px wide (dashed pink box in the renders). At 360px some words cannot fit unsplit. Horizontal scrolling is ALLOWED: the table may be wider than 360px (column widths summing to more than 359px) (the reader scrolls), or you may fit within 359px and accept the consequences. Fitting and scrolling layouts are judged as two separate classes; propose good layouts of BOTH kinds.
Rendering convention: a full render shows the WHOLE table; anything right of the dashed box is not clipped — it is reached by scrolling. Where a layout scrolls, an extra "viewport view" image shows only what is visible at first sight.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. Only the column widths are designed; row heights follow from them.

Your understanding: {"purpose":"Connect each incident with its trace identifier, severity and plain-language description.","tasks":["Find an incident by its incident or trace ID.","Check its severity and understand what happened.","Compare incidents across the three records."],"relations":["Each row is one incident; its ID, trace ID, severity and summary belong together.","The incident ID and trace ID are distinct identifiers, while severity qualifies the incident and the summary describes it."],"roles":["The header row names four fields.","Incident is the practical row identifier, although no row header is formally declared.","Trace ID is a lookup and correlation key; Severity is a short categorical field; Summary is explanatory prose."],"keep_whole":["Incident IDs and trace IDs should remain intact for reliable lookup and copying.","Severity codes and their header should remain intact.","Individual words should remain whole where space permits."],"may_wrap":["Summary prose may wrap naturally between words.","In a viewport-fitting layout, long identifiers and some words must split because their combined minimum widths exceed the available space."],"same_scale":["Incident and trace identifiers need stable, readable fields, but the longer trace IDs require more width.","Severity needs only a compact field; Summary benefits from flexible space for prose."],"h_vs_v":"A fitting table avoids horizontal scrolling but forces identifier breaks and tall rows. A wider table preserves identifiers and improves row scanning, at the cost of scrolling between the identifying fields and the summary; giving prose still more width reduces row height but increases that travel."}

Image 1 is the one-line content overview. Then real browser renders of: d3r0A, d3r0B (full view, then viewport view), d3r0C (full view, then viewport view).
Measured facts:
d3r0A: column widths [100, 96, 80, 83] px · table 360×751 px · row heights [60, 339, 199, 153] · column headers on >1 line: 1/4 · tallest cell 14 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 13 · fits the 360 px viewport (no scrolling)
d3r0B: column widths [165, 299, 80, 250] px · table 795×262 px · row heights [36, 106, 60, 60] · column headers on >1 line: 0/4 · tallest cell 4 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 0 · WIDER than the viewport by 435 px (horizontal scrolling)
d3r0C: column widths [165, 299, 80, 712] px · table 1257×146 px · row heights [36, 36, 36, 36] · column headers on >1 line: 0/4 · tallest cell 1 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 0 · WIDER than the viewport by 897 px (horizontal scrolling)

Look at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design: what works, what is visually wrong, and the cause (which width). This is your first look at real renders: propose at least one improved or alternative design (refine the most promising, fix what you saw, or test an important idea you have not tried). "done" is not allowed yet. Do not resubmit near-identical widths.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"best":["your best design name(s) so far"],"done":false,"designs":[{"widths":[int px],"change":"what and why"}]}
